text: BEA-level marginal totals were sourced from PUWS only in instances where total flows between BEA regions exceeded FAF totals. For flows where FAF totals were higher, it was assumed that PUWS flows were suppressed and therefore not updated in combined dataset. Once the marginal totals were obtained, iterative proportional 46 fitting was employed to disaggregate the dataset to county level. This statistical technique updates the county-level data by ensuring consistency with the known totals from the combined dataset. After estimating county-level OD movements for rail freight, the future movements were projected by applying FAF growth factors specific to each Standard Classification of Transported Goods (SCTG) code (USDOT, 2017). SCTG is the federal standard for classifying freight shipments in the US. These growth factors, derived from the FAF, proportionally increase or decrease projected freight flows based on anticipated changes in commodity demand and transportation patterns. This approach allows for more realistic projections of future rail freight movements by considering the unique growth trajectories for each commodity. Further, a multistep process was employed to estimate the total ton-miles of freight transported by rail in each state. First, county-level OD movements were integrated into the rail network. This involved identifying the nearest node in the network to each county’s centroid, effectively connecting the shipment data to the physical rail infrastructure. Next, using a shortest path algorithm, the route between each OD pair was estimated, assigning all tons between the origin and destination counties to that specific route. The final tons transported on each rail segment, or link, were calculated by summing all the tons assigned to that link from various OD movements. Finally, the ton-miles for each state were determined by multiplying the total tons transported on each rail segment within the state by the segment’s length. To streamline the analysis and maintain a focus on the U.S. system, the routing process was limited to tracks within the NARN designated as “Main Line” or “Major Industrial Lead,” and excluding rail tracks from Canada and Mexico (BTS, 2025). In addition, the network was only segmented at interchanges or nodes connecting different states, simplifying the analysis while ensuring the accurate representation of interstate freight flows. 5.2.3 Estimation of Distillate Fuel Oil Use by Rail by State To estimate state-level distillate fuel oil consumption by rail, ton-mile data were used as an independent variable. The known railroad distillate fuel oil consumption data from the EIA for 2017–2020 served as the response variable. Multiple regression models, including linear, ridge, lasso, decision tree, and support vector regression, were evaluated to identify the most accurate predictive model. The model with the highest cross-validation score was ultimately selected to forecast future distillate fuel oil consumption by state. 5.2.4 Results on Estimation of Energy Use by Top Corridors Using the OD movements between counties from the combined dataset and implementing Shortest Path algorithm, link-level tonnages were estimated for the year 2017.
